### Observed differences

- Resource allocation changed on many activities. In the earlier window, activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 were each handled by a broad set of codes whose largest single shares were about 3–10 in 100 (for example User_69 at 8–10 in 100); in the later window a largely different set took over, led by User_98 with about 13–20 in 100 of each activity's assignments, while most earlier leading codes dropped out of the top group. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, ASSIGN008]
- A08 and A11 show the same kind of replacement: the earlier leading codes (about 12–13 in 100 each) fell to roughly 5–6 in 100 or below, and a new set led by User_133 at about 17 in 100 took over; the later profile rests on 93 cases versus 112 earlier. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]
- A04 became fully concentrated: earlier its assignments were spread over 29 distinct codes with the largest holding about 48 in 100 (concentration index 0.24); later a single code handled all of them (share 100 in 100, index 1.0). [CONC001]
- A09 ran in more cases: about 57 in 100 earlier (113 of 200 traces) against about 71 in 100 later (142 of 200), with no within-case repetition in either window. Consistently, among A05's observed outgoing transitions the share going to A09 rose from about 57 to 71 in 100, while the share going to A04 fell from about 44 to 29 in 100. [OCC001, DIR001]
- A16's outgoing flow was redistributed: the share to A11 fell from about 29 to 12 in 100, while shares to A07 rose from about 31 to 40, to A10 from about 11 to 16 and to A24 from about 21 to 23; A02 appears as a successor only in the later window, in under 1 in 100 transitions (about one case). [DIR002]
- A04 appears slightly later within cases (median relative position about 0.12 earlier versus 0.14 later); this is an event-position measure, not clock time. [POS001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that work was reallocated to a largely different set of resources. In the earlier window, eight activities (A01, A03, A08, A11, A13, A14, A17, A22) were each spread over many codes with low individual shares, and in the later window six of them are dominated by a new group led by User_98 (about 13–20 in 100), A08 and A11 by a group led by User_133 (about 17 in 100), while A04 went from 29 sharing codes to a single code handling every case. This rests on direct allocation evidence: the resource family produced 9 qualifying items against about 0.006 expected for an unchanged process, every item points in the same direction, and each difference is larger than in at least 999.5 of 1000 random re-splits. Limitations: the codes are anonymous and the indicators show shares only, so the evidence cannot distinguish a change in allocation rules from a change in which resources were available in each window, and the identical profiles of the A13/A14 and A08/A11 pairs mean the items are not independent confirmations. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, ASSIGN008, CONC001]

Other differences: Control flow also shifted, and the evidence does not show whether this is connected to the reallocation. A09 took part in about 15 more cases per 100 (57 to 71 in 100), and A05's flow moved towards A09 and away from A04 (44 to 29 in 100), with both alternative successors still well observed in both windows — a shift in how often existing paths are taken rather than a replaced path. A16's flow shifted from A11 towards A07, A10 and A24. A04 also appears slightly later within cases (median relative position about 0.12 to 0.14), a small position shift that by itself does not show the activity was moved. The control-flow family produced 4 qualifying items against about 0.21 expected by chance. [OCC001, DIR001, DIR002, POS001]
